note: The Browser Company's 21-second spot for Tidy Tabs, the Arc feature that sorts a messy sidebar into labeled groups. The whole script is nine words on Arc blue: 'Don't worry. Tab freely. Tidy Tabs. Now available in Arc.' Between them, the sidebar fills with tabs, a click on a broom icon turns a divider into a wavy line, and the tabs fall into groups. Then it happens again in three other people's Spaces, full of that week's Super Bowl, Grammys and Vision Pro tabs. The breakdown follows how a demo is told in one long take and then repeated as fast proof, and samples 11 moves as flip books.
no_transcript: No speech. Whisper heard only hallucinated lines ('Music', 'Thank you.'), and the voice-like layer the separator finds from 13.5 s is part of the music, with no words. The script is nine words of on-screen text; the Craft map lays them out.

shot_notes.0: 'Don't worry' in heavy white sans on flat Arc blue (about #124CF6). 'Don't' appears at 0.17 and 'worry' at 0.5, one word per beat. The film reassures before it has shown any problem.
shot_notes.1: A hard cut to Arc's sidebar, magnified so one tab row is about the height of a headline. A photo of a pine forest shows through on the left, a sliver of white page sits on the right, and the pointer rests out on the page. One tab so far: 'The 15 Best Vacuum Cl…'.
shot_notes.2: Tabs keep arriving at the bottom of the list and the view scrolls down with them: vacuum reviews, the 2024 Oscars, tips for a visit to San Diego. This is the rabbit hole from the video's description, shown and never said.
shot_notes.3: Zoo lists, a site called Sebo, more Oscars. The tabs have nothing in common, which is the point. New rows fade up from transparent rather than sliding in.
shot_notes.4: Back to blue for 'Tab', alone. It is used as a verb, which is Arc's voice: tabbing is something you do, like browsing.
shot_notes.5: 'Tab freely', with 'freely' set in italic. The only styled word in the film, and the permission the ad is selling.
shot_notes.6: Close on the top of the sidebar: 'Clear' with a small broom icon, and the pointer on it. The divider line to its left has started to ripple. The film puts the camera right on the one control that matters.
shot_notes.7: The camera has pulled back to show the sidebar beside an article page ('The Best…', a vacuum review), still with the same unsorted tabs. The pull-back gives the viewer the whole list just before it changes.
shot_notes.8: Sorted. The same tabs now sit under small grey labels, 'Vacuum Shopping', 'Movies' and 'San Diego Zoo', with the tab you were on kept at the top. Nothing else on screen has changed, so the change reads at a glance.
shot_notes.9: 'Tidy Tabs' on blue: the feature's name arrives only after the viewer has watched it work once. It fades up in a few frames instead of cutting on.
shot_notes.10: A second Space, in salmon with a black-and-white mountain wallpaper. The same close-up of 'Clear' and the same pointer, framed almost identically to the first, so the second demo is recognized instantly.
shot_notes.11: Wide on the salmon Space beside a CBS Sports article, mid-sort: Super Bowl 58, Valentine's Day lists and Grammys tabs settling under their labels. The film skipped the wait by cutting away from the close-up while the line was still wavy.
shot_notes.12: A third Space in teal over a painted sky: Universal Studios tips, a Vision Pro durability video and Mario games, still mixed. The open page is a blurred YouTube video of a man talking, so it reads as someone's real browsing, not a staged page.
shot_notes.13: The teal list sorted into 'Universal Studios', 'Vision Pro' and 'Nintendo Games'. Each wide shot starts messy and ends sorted within about half a second.
shot_notes.14: A fourth Space in orange over a dark forest: a white lamp product page, with tabs sorted into 'Lamp Shopping', 'Oppenheimer' and 'Arc Browser'. One of the groups is Arc's own launch video, a quiet in-joke.
shot_notes.15: 'Now available in Arc' on blue, the longest line in the film and the only one that is plain information.
shot_notes.16: Back to a close-up: a pinned 'letterboxd' tab above the teal Space's 'Clear', the pointer under the broom, the divider just starting to ripple. The film returns to the button one more time instead of ending on a result.
shot_notes.17: The Arc logo, a white looping line drawing, alone on blue. The cut comes while the divider is still wavy, so the last product image is the feature working, not finished.
shot_notes.19: 'arc.net' replaces the logo at about 18.7 and holds to the end, in the same white sans as the rest of the copy.

motion_intro: Every shot is either a flat blue card with a few words or a magnified piece of Arc's sidebar. There is no camera in a physical sense: the 'moves' are scrolls, one pull-back from a close-up, and the interface's own animations. Three of those carry the film. New tabs fade up at the bottom of the list. The divider beside 'Clear' turns into a moving wavy line while the feature works. And the rows rearrange into groups in about a third of a second, with small grey labels appearing between them. The first demo plays these in one take; the later ones are cut so the viewer sees only the click or only the sort, never the wait.

motion.title: Two words, one at a time
motion.text: The film opens on empty blue. 'Don't' appears at 0.17, already centered, and 'worry' is added at 0.5, the pair re-centering as a block. Neither word animates; each simply arrives. At 1.30 a hard cut throws us into the sidebar.

motion.title: Tabs pile up and the list scrolls with them
motion.text: One tab at 1.33, a second at about 1.67, a third fading up at 2.0 and solid by 2.17, then a San Diego zoo list at 2.67, Sebo at 3.33, another zoo tab at 3.5 and an Oscars tab ghosting in at 3.83. As each one lands, the view scrolls down so the newest row stays in frame and the oldest leave off the top; 'New Tab' is gone by 2.0. The pointer never moves from the page on the right. The pile is shown as something that just happens to you while you read.

motion.title: 'Tab', then 'freely' in italic
motion.text: Cut to blue at 4.37 with 'Tab' alone in the middle. At about 4.8 'freely' is added in italic and the line re-centers. Same rule as the opening: words arrive whole, the block keeps itself centered. Cut to the close-up at 5.54.

motion.title: Click, ripple, pull back, sort
motion.text: The close-up holds on 'Clear' with the pointer coming up to the broom at 5.67. The broom darkens as it is pressed around 6.0. From 6.33 the thin divider to its left starts to ripple and spreads into a wavy line. At about 6.4 the view starts to pull back and keeps shrinking until about 7.3, so the whole unsorted list and the page beside it come into frame while the line is still wavy. At 7.5 the tabs rearrange into three labeled groups in one or two frames. One continuous take covers the whole feature: the button, the wait and the result.

motion.title: The name fades up
motion.text: At 8.54 the blue card opens on 'Tidy Tabs' at low opacity, solid by about 8.67, a faster and softer entrance than the other words get. It holds for a second and cuts at 9.68 to the next close-up.

motion.title: The same close-up, a different Space
motion.text: The salmon Space is framed like the first close-up, with 'Clear' top right and two tabs below. The pointer sits on the broom from 9.67; the divider starts to ripple at about 10.5 and is a full wavy line by 10.75. At 10.84 the film cuts to a wide shot before any tab has moved, so the waiting part of the feature is left in this shot and the result goes to the next.

motion.title: Super Bowl, Valentine's Day, Grammys
motion.text: The wide shot opens on the unsorted list next to a CBS Sports article on Super Bowl predictions. At about 11.3 the rows shuffle and grey labels open up between them, and by 11.42 the list reads 'Super Bowl', 'Valentine's Day', 'Grammys'. It then holds for most of a second so the labels can be read before the cut at 12.18.

motion.title: Universal Studios, Vision Pro, Nintendo Games
motion.text: A teal Space over a painted sky, with a talking-head YouTube video open. The shot starts already mid-trip and with no close-up before it: Universal tips, a Vision Pro durability test and Mario titles mixed together. From about 12.42 the rows scatter and settle, and by 12.58 they sit under 'Universal Studios', 'Vision Pro' and 'Nintendo Games'. No click is shown at all; by the third time, the film trusts the viewer to supply it.

motion.title: Lamp Shopping, Oppenheimer, Arc Browser
motion.text: An orange Space over a dark forest, beside a product page for a white ceramic lamp. The list holds unsorted until about 13.92, then reorders in about two frames, and from 14.0 reads 'Lamp Shopping', 'Oppenheimer' and 'Arc Browser'. The sort comes later in this shot than in the last, about 0.4 s in rather than 0.25, then holds until the cut to 'Now available in Arc' at 14.88.

motion.title: End on the wait, not the result
motion.text: A close-up of the teal Space, with a pinned 'letterboxd' tab above 'Clear'. The pointer is under the broom at 16.08 and the divider begins to ripple at about 16.42, a full wave by 16.58. The pointer drifts left along the wave while it moves. The cut to the logo comes at 17.35 with the line still wavy: the film's last product image is the feature at work.

motion.title: Logo, then the address
motion.text: The Arc logo appears at 17.35, a white looping line on the same blue, and holds still for over a second. At about 18.7 it is swapped on a single frame for 'arc.net', which holds to the end at 20.5. No animation on the logo and no tagline: the address is the call to action.

lede: A twenty-one second ad for one feature. Tidy Tabs is a button at the top of Arc's sidebar that sorts your open tabs into labeled groups. The film has no voice and nine words of copy, set one or two at a time on Arc's blue: 'Don't worry', 'Tab freely', 'Tidy Tabs', 'Now available in Arc'. Everything else is the sidebar itself, magnified until a tab row is as big as a headline.

What is worth learning is how it demonstrates a feature that takes a moment to run. The first demo is one take: tabs pile up, a click, the divider ripples while it works, the camera pulls back, and the tabs fall into groups. After that the film shows the feature three more times in other people's Spaces, and it cuts each repeat down to just the click or just the sort. The viewer learns the whole thing once and then sees proof that it works on anyone's mess.

aspects.title: The answer comes before the problem
paragraphs: The film opens on 'Don't worry' before there is anything to worry about. Only then do the tabs start piling up, and the next card is 'Tab freely'. The usual order for a feature ad is problem, then solution. Here the comfort comes first, so the mess that follows reads as harmless: you are being told to go ahead and make it. The YouTube description says the missing half out loud ('Going down a rabbit hole? Don't worry, tab freely'), but the film leaves the rabbit hole to the picture.

The name comes third. 'Tidy Tabs' appears only after the viewer has watched it work once, so the name labels something already understood instead of introducing something to be explained. 'Now available in Arc' and 'arc.net' close it out. There is no description of how it works, no mention of AI, and no benefit stated in words beyond 'tab freely'.

moments.text: 'Don't worry', before anything has gone wrong.
The rabbit hole: vacuums, the Oscars, the zoo.
The name, after the first demo.

aspects.title: One full demo, then three fast repeats
paragraphs: The first demonstration runs for three seconds without a cut. It starts close on 'Clear' and its broom icon, the pointer presses it, and the divider beside it turns into a moving wavy line, Arc's sign that the feature is working. While the line is still wavy, the view pulls back so the whole unsorted list is visible next to the page. Then the tabs rearrange into 'Vacuum Shopping', 'Movies' and 'San Diego Zoo'. Because the shot never cuts, the viewer can trust that this is what the button does, wait included.

The repeats are edited down. The salmon Space gets the close-up and the wavy line, then cuts to the wide shot just before the sort. The teal and orange Spaces get no click at all, only a wide shot that starts messy and is sorted within half a second. By then the viewer knows what caused it. Each repeat is about 1.2 to 1.4 seconds, so in five seconds the film shows three more sorts without asking the viewer to wait through the feature again.

The interface is shown huge. In the close-ups a tab title is set as large as the title cards, and even the wide shots show only the sidebar and a slice of the page. The rest of the browser, the address bar and the window chrome never appear. The film shows the one part of the product the feature touches and enlarges it until it is legible on a phone.

moments.text: The click, and the divider starting to ripple.

aspects.title: Tabs from that week
paragraphs: The film came out on 7 February 2024, and the tabs belong to that week: Super Bowl 58 predictions, Valentine's Day lists, the Grammys, a Vision Pro durability test a few days after the headset shipped, Oppenheimer during awards season. Each Space is a plausible person on a plausible day, which does more than generic placeholder tabs would to make the mess feel like the viewer's own.

Each Space also has its own color and wallpaper (sage over a pine forest, salmon over a misty mountain, teal over a painted sky, orange over a dark forest), which is how Arc users really tell their Spaces apart. The colors make the repeats read as different people at a glance, and they rhyme with the flat blue cards, so the whole film looks like one palette. One of the sorted groups is 'Arc Browser', with Arc's own launch video in it.

aspects.title: Cards and screens, cut in turns
paragraphs: The film alternates strictly between two kinds of shot: a flat blue card with one or two words, and the sidebar. No shot mixes them; the copy never sits over the product. Each card holds for about a second, long enough for a few words, and the words arrive whole and re-center rather than animating. The one exception is 'Tidy Tabs', which fades up, giving the name a slightly different entrance from the rest of the copy.

After the first three-second demo the cutting settles into an even pace: from 8.54 to 17.35 every shot lasts between 1.13 and 1.37 seconds. The music is not what sets it; cuts do not land on the estimated beat more often than chance. The film stops its product footage on the wavy line, cutting to the logo while the feature is still working, so the last thing in the sidebar is the button doing its job.

moments.text: A card: one word, nothing else.
The close-up framed to match the first one.
The last product shot, still mid-sort.
The logo cuts in on the wave.

patterns.name: Reassure before you show the problem
patterns.text: Open on the comforting line ('Don't worry') and then show the mess. The problem plays as something the viewer is allowed to do, not something they should fear.

patterns.name: Demo once in a single take
patterns.text: Show the feature end to end without a cut the first time, including its working state, so the viewer trusts it is real.

patterns.name: Then repeat it with the wait cut out
patterns.text: After the full demo, show it on other people's data with only the click or only the result. Repetition proves it generalizes; editing keeps it fast.

patterns.name: Name the feature after it has been seen
patterns.text: Put the product name on screen right after the first demo, so it labels something the viewer already understands.

patterns.name: Fill the demo with this week's tabs
patterns.text: Stock the demo with whatever people are actually reading right now. Placeholder content looks staged; topical content looks like the viewer's own browser.

patterns.name: Magnify the one control
patterns.text: Crop to the part of the interface the feature touches and scale it up until a single row is headline size. Drop the rest of the window.

craft.absent: There is no voice, no person on camera, no explanation of how the sorting works and no mention of AI. The music is a steady bed that the picture is not cut to. Study it for how to demonstrate a one-button feature fast: one honest take, then quick repeats.
